Welcome

Balance Service, Cost, and Capital.

Supply chains are expected to satisfy customers, control operating cost, and avoid tying up too much cash. In practice, strengthening one objective usually creates pressure on at least one of the others.

Service

Availability, responsiveness, reliability, and customer satisfaction.

Cost

Purchasing, production, transportation, and operating expenses.

Capital

Inventory, capacity, assets, and cash tied up in the supply chain.

iFor each of five situations, position the priority pin and then choose the operational action that best reflects that balance.
Remember: the appropriate position changes with the company, product, customer, and immediate situation.

Key takeaway

The best balance changes with the business situation.

The movement of your five pins is the point. Effective supply chain management requires priorities to be adjusted rather than fixed permanently.

✓ Five situations completed

More Service

Often requires additional inventory, capacity, flexibility, premium transport, or other responsive operations.

Lower Cost

May require standardisation, consolidation, larger batches, or reduced responsiveness.

Lower Capital

Often means leaner inventory and fewer assets, which can increase exposure to operational risk.

Effective supply chain management is not about maximising one corner in isolation. It is about choosing—and continually adjusting—the balance that best supports the business situation.
